content: A tooth abscess is a localized collection of pus that forms within the tissues of the jawbone, typically at the tip of an infected tooth. This condition is most often caused by a bacterial infection that accumulates in the soft pulp tissue of the tooth. It is frequently associated with a dull, throbbing, and severe pain, although this is not always the case. There are two primary types of dental abscesses. A periapical abscess originates in the dental pulp, which is the innermost part of the tooth containing nerves and blood vessels. In contrast, a periodontal abscess begins in the supporting structures of the teeth, such as the bone and surrounding tissues. The development of a tooth abscess is often linked to the presence of dead pulp tissue. Common risk factors include tooth decay, cracked or fractured teeth, advanced periodontal disease, and complications from a failed root canal treatment. If left untreated, a severe tooth abscess can grow in size and potentially perforate the surrounding bone, spreading into adjacent soft tissues. The infection typically follows the path of least resistance, which may lead to either internal or external spread. The direction of the infection is influenced by factors such as the location of the affected tooth and the thickness of the surrounding bone, muscles, and fascia. External drainage may manifest as a boil that eventually bursts, allowing pus to drain either intraorally (through the gum) or extraorally. Chronic drainage can result in the formation of a fistula, which is a canal lined with epithelial tissue that facilitates the continuous drainage of pus. Internal drainage, however, is more concerning, as the infection can expand within the surrounding tissues. Severe complications may arise, necessitating immediate hospitalization. One such complication is Ludwig's angina, a life-threatening condition characterized by a rapidly spreading infection and cellulitis that can obstruct the airway, potentially leading to suffocation. Additionally, the infection may spread downward into the mediastinum, a central compartment in the chest, posing significant risks to vital organs such as the heart. Infections originating from upper teeth may also lead to septicemia (blood infection) due to their proximity to blood vessels. Although rare, a brain abscess is another potential complication. Depending on the severity of the infection, symptoms can range from mild discomfort to life-threatening conditions requiring urgent medical intervention. The most common symptom of an acute tooth abscess is a persistent, throbbing toothache at the site of the infection. In some cases, the abscess may perforate the bone and drain into the surrounding tissues, causing localized facial swelling. Swollen and tender lymph nodes in the neck may also occur as the body responds to the infection. Treatment for a tooth abscess typically involves addressing the source of the infection. One option is tooth extraction, which removes the infected tooth entirely. In certain cases, however, the tooth may be saved through root canal therapy, which involves cleaning and disinfecting the pulp chamber and root canal system. In more severe cases, invasive surgical intervention may be required. This may involve accessing the abscess through the cheek, removing the infected tooth, and inserting a drainage tube to allow any remaining pus to exit.
